metadata.title: Key Information and Facilitating Understanding in Informed Consent Guidance for Sponsors, Investigators, and Institutional Review Boards
metadata.topic: Draft guideline · FDA human drugs and biologics
metadata.legal_basis: FDA Guidance Document (21 CFR 10.115). Guidance states FDA's current thinking and is not binding unless a statute or regulation requires it; the official text governs.

candidates.statement: 4 This guidance applies to FDA-regulated clinical investigations of drugs, biologics, or devices that are subject to 21 CFR parts 50 and 56, including investigations under 21 CFR parts 312 and 812. This guidance also applies to HHS- supported or -conducted nonexempt human subjects research that is subject to 45 CFR part 46. As used in this guidance, an investigational medical product is an investigational drug or biological product as defined in 21 CFR part 312 or an investigational device as defined in 21 CFR part 812.

candidates.statement: The presentation of key information at the beginning of the consent process can help facilitate 73 discussions between a prospective subject and an investigator about whether the prospective 74 subject should participate in the trial. This information also may be useful to enrolled subjects as 75 a resource and to facilitate any further discussions with investigators. We recommend that the 76 key information section of a consent document 11 be relatively short (e.g., generally no more than 77 a few pages). A sample key information section of a consent form for a hypothetical clinical trial 78 is included in the appendix of this guidance. The format of the sample is based, in part, on 79 research regarding how the presentation of information may affect consumers’ understanding of 80 FDA’s proposed rule and in this guidance means “harmonize to the extent practicable and consistent with other statutory provisions,” consistent with section 3023 of the 21st Century Cures Act (Cures Act) (Public Law 114-255).
candidates.context: The revised Common Rule requires consent information to “begin with a concise and focused 67 presentation of the key information that is most likely to assist a prospective subject or legally 68 authorized representative in understanding the reasons why one might or might not want to 69 participate in the research” (45 CFR 46.116(a)(5)(i)). FDA’s proposed regulations would add 70 identical language to 21 CFR 50.20(e)(1). 71 Some HHS-supported or -conducted research is not subject to the revised Common Rule per 45 CFR 46.101(l)(3) and is not required to address the provisions of the revised Common Rule addressed in this guidance.

For research that is not FDA-regulated and is carried out under OHRP’s Emergency Research Consent Waiver provisions (61 FR 51531-51533, October 2, 1996) for research where obtaining informed consent from subjects or their legally authorized representatives is not feasible, there is no key information requirement. Where consent is feasible, the consent process and documents must satisfy the key information requirement.

candidates.statement: Which basic and additional consent elements should be included in the key information section 129 may vary based on factors such as the study attributes and its design; the condition(s), 130 behavior(s), or outcome(s) being examined; and the prospective subject population. Basic and 131 additional elements (or parts of such elements) of informed consent that are not addressed (or not 132 fully addressed) in the key information section would need to be included elsewhere in the 133 consent form as required (21 CFR 50.25(a) and (b) and 45 CFR 46.116(b) and (c)). 134
candidates.context: One approach to developing the content of the key information section is for prospective subjects 123 and other interested parties to advise on which basic and additional elements of informed consent 124 may be considered “key” from the perspective of prospective subjects for a particular study. We 125 recommend that the most important elements for a particular study be included at the beginning 126 of the key information section. 127 If appropriate, the elements of informed consent that are addressed in the key information section 136 can also be repeated in other parts of the consent form. For instance, information about the most 137 important reasonably foreseeable risks (e.g., most serious and/or most common adverse events) 138 could be addressed in the key information section and could also be repeated with 139 comprehensive risk information later in the consent form. candidates.statement: The discussion of risks and discomforts is generally among one of the most important and 216 complex required elements of informed consent, and we recommend that this topic be addressed 217 in the key information section. We recommend providing information about the most common 218 and serious risks and discomforts in the key information section to inform a prospective subject’s 219 decision about participation. 21 Key information about risks and discomforts of research 220 participation should be included on the first page of the key information section, if possible. If 221 the key information section does not include all risk-related information, the key information 222 section should note that fact and include a page cross-reference (or hyperlink for electronic 223 documents) that directs prospective subjects to the appropriate section of the consent form where 224 complete information is located. 225

candidates.statement: Any reasonably expected benefits of participating in research, either to prospective subjects or 251 others, are likely to be considered key information and could be a major determinant of whether 252 a prospective subject decides to participate in a study. If there is no potential for direct benefit to 253 the prospective subject, this point should be clearly stated. In general, for clinical research, it is 254 important that prospective subjects understand that research is not the same as clinical care and 255 that there may be considerable uncertainty about any potential benefits. 24 Details about any 256 potential benefits of participation in a study should be presented in a manner that does not 257 convey an inappropriate or overly optimistic representation of the facts. Potential benefits 258 should be explained in terms of any direct impact to the prospective subject, in addition to the 259

candidates.statement: In many circumstances, key information should include a clear and concise description of 277 alternative procedures or courses of treatment, if any, that might be appropriate for the 278 prospective subject. For clinical studies, consider first informing prospective subjects about care 279 they would likely receive if not involved in the study and then providing them with information 280 to help them understand how the care they would receive in the study differs. The emphasis 281 should be on increasing awareness of alternatives because the choice between available 282 alternatives is expected to vary based on individual values and preferences. 283

candidates.statement: We recommend that interested parties consider whether the key information section should also 304 address costs the prospective subject may incur when participating in a study. If the sponsor or 305 investigator intends to charge for the cost of tests, procedures, products, and/or interventions 306 (including interventions outside of a clinical setting) used during the study, information about 307 costs that may be incurred by a prospective subject or whether the prospective subject’s health 308 insurance could be charged (along with information on how to determine whether health 309 insurance will cover costs) should be included in the key information section. The key 310 information section could also inform prospective subjects about whether they will be 311 reimbursed for study-related expenses (e.g., mileage, parking, airfare, lodging, childcare) 312 because such information may influence a prospective subject’s decision to participate. 313 Similarly, incentives to encourage participation, as well as payments for a prospective subject’s 314 time, inconvenience, and/or discomfort, may be appropriate to include as key information. 315

For example, will it reduce options for standard treatments, prevent 342 prospective subjects from accessing future care or from participating in other studies, or 343 impact personal activities such as driving or sun exposure? 344 (5) How will a prospective subject’s experience in this study differ from treatment outside of 345 the study? 346 (6) How is this research novel? 347 (7) What investigator’s conflict of interest (if any) may be of interest to prospective subjects? 348 (8) How can prospective subjects access any investigational medical products or other 349 interventions examined in the study following completion of the study? 350 The answers to these and similar questions can be used to help identify information that could be 351 appropriate to include with the key information for a given study. candidates.statement: Information should be presented in plain language and at a level prospective subjects would 444 likely comprehend; explanations should be included for scientific and medical terms. 41 An 445 assessment of the needs and characteristics of the prospective subject population, including their 446 age, any relevant medical diagnosis, level of English proficiency, education level, and cognitive 447 abilities, can be helpful in developing consent information that facilitates understanding. 448 Information should be provided in the primary language of a prospective subject with limited 449 English proficiency. 42 Although not required, one possible way to evaluate whether the 450 information is presented in a way that facilitates understanding is to have the information 451 reviewed by individuals unfamiliar with the research. This may be particularly helpful for forms 452 translated into additional languages. For example, this could include review by patient advocacy 453 groups or a sample of individuals from the subject population. 454

candidates.statement: 42 FDA and OHRP strongly encourage stakeholders to ensure that informed consent documents are accessible to individuals with limited English proficiency. To the extent an organization receives Federal financial assistance from HHS, the organization must comply with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and its implementing regulations. This guidance provides information to assist IRBs, investigators, and sponsors in complying with OHRP’s regulation and FDA’s proposed regulation, if and when it is finalized, related to the key information section of informed consent. This document does not provide guidance on how to comply with any regulatory obligations stemming from a source outside of the statutes FDA and OHRP administer and their respective regulations.

candidates.statement: Voluntary Participation and Right to Discontinue Participation We are asking you to consent to participate in this research study. Your participation is voluntary and should be based on what is important to you. It is your choice to participate in this trial. If you agree to participate, you may leave at any time without penalty or loss of benefits to which you are otherwise entitled.
candidates.context: Key Information You Should Know Before Agreeing to Participate The key information that follows can help you learn more about this clinical trial. It can also help you decide whether or not to take part in the trial. Please read the entire consent form or have someone read it with you. If there is anything that you do not understand, please talk to the trial doctor or team to have your questions answered before signing the consent form.
